records.text: Riddle: how many targets can one piece hit? Here, several at once. That's a fork, and usually only one target gets away.
Puzzle piece: after this move, one enemy piece can land on a square that hits several targets together. Forks grow out of squares like that.
Which move had the fork? Wrong suspect: a different move put one piece on several targets at once.
Why can't that piece move? Somewhere behind it on the same line sits its king. Pinned, neat and tidy.
Spot the line: the other side can now freeze one of the pieces in front of its own king, and that piece would be glued to it.
Missed clue: another move set up a pin, sticking a piece in front of its own king. This one leaves that idea alone.
Front piece attacked, so it steps aside, and what's waiting behind it? A second victim. Skewer!
Zoom in on that line: two pieces stacked on it, and now the other side can skewer them. Chase the front one, and the back one hangs.
The kicker was a skewer: a different move would have chased the front piece off its line and left the one behind it hanging.
Riddle time: the guard on that piece just got captured. So who's on duty now? Nobody.
Notice the guard: a defender can be captured by the other side now, and whatever it protects would lose its cover.
Which move takes out the defender? Another culprit entirely; this move leaves that guard on duty.
Where can that king run? Nowhere; its own pieces block it in. This move aims right at the back rank.
Zoom in on the king's exits: its own pieces block them, and a back-rank mate is now in reach for the other side.
X marks the back rank: another move had mate against a king walled in by its own pieces. Here, the move points elsewhere.
How far to the last rank? Hardly any squares left. Once that pawn arrives, it becomes a new piece.
Pawn race: one of their pawns has an open road to the last rank now, and promotion is a real threat.
Missed clue: a stronger move would have cleared a pawn's road to the last rank. This move keeps that pawn stuck behind the traffic.
Which piece was the real attacker? The hidden one! Its blocker slides away, and the attack behind it switches on.
Zoom in: two of their pieces share a line, and if the front one steps aside, the one behind it attacks. Discovered attack incoming.
The hidden attacker stayed hidden: in a different move, one piece would have stepped aside to let the one behind it strike.
One move, a pair of riddles for the defense, and usually just one gets answered. Double attack!
Here's the kicker: one reply now gives the other side two threats at once, and parrying both is tricky.
A stronger move made two threats at once, a double attack, and this move leaves it on the table.
What was that defender's job? Guarding a key square. Lure it away, and the square opens up. Deflection!
Spot the busy piece: that defender has an important job, and the other side can now drag it away from its post.
Which move pulled the defender off its job? Another one, not this. Here, the defender keeps guarding.
Count the guards on that piece: zero. So it comes off the board for free.
Which move grabbed the loose piece? Look elsewhere: that piece had zero defenders. Quick check before every move: anything loose?
Count the defenders on that piece: zero. It's simply there for the other side to take.
Found the detail! One defender was holding that piece up, and this move marches it off duty, so the other side can capture. Quick check before a defender moves: what's it holding up?
Rewind one move and it clicks: their last move made a threat, nobody dealt with it, and now a piece can be captured. First question every turn: what's their threat?
That first capture looks tasty, but here's the kicker: the recapture wins back more. Tally both sides of every trade before diving in.
Telltale sign of a good start: a minor piece steps out from where it began.
A different move would have woken up a minor piece and got it out from its original square.
Not a single pawn on that file, from either side. The rook gets every square of it.
A different move could have given a rook a totally pawn-free file.
Scan the rook's file: zero pawns of its own, one or more of the enemy's. Semi-open!
A different move had a semi-open file ready for a rook, no pawns of its own, at least one enemy pawn on it.
Can any enemy pawn stop it? Not on its file, and not on the files beside it. Passed pawn!
A different move would have made a passed pawn, one that no enemy pawn could block or take on the way up.
One more square for the passed pawn, creeping toward the far end of the board.
A different move would have marched the passed pawn one step closer to queening.
Look left, look right: no friendly pawn next door on either side. That pawn's an island.
A different move would have cut a pawn off from its friends, with no pawn of its color next door on either side.
A loose end gets tied up: the lonely piece picks up a protector.
A different move would have given an unguarded piece some protection.
Mental note: this piece is out there with no guard now. Not lost, but worth tracking.
A different move would have left a piece unguarded, though being unguarded doesn't make it winnable.
Telltale sign of safety: the king picks up another square it can legally use.
A different move would have given the king another legal hidey-hole.
Castling: two squares for the king, and the rook jumps over to land right next to it.
Castling was on the table too, moving king and rook to new squares in a single turn.
Pair broken: after this capture, one side's remaining bishops stick to a single color.
A different move would have nabbed one of the bishops, breaking up the other side's pair.
Telltale sign: same color, same file, two pawns in a column. Doubled.
A different move would have put two same-colored pawns on one file, one in front of the other.
Spotlight on the king: after this, the other side gets a mating attack that can't be stopped. Where did its safety slip away? Let's trace it back.
X marks the spot: a forced checkmate was ready, and this move slides right past it. Want to find the mating line?
A sacrifice that holds up! The material is there for the taking, yet in the line we checked, the idea survives the capture.
One key, one lock: of the moves we checked, every other one was losing, and only this keeps the position playable.
The one move that keeps the edge: the rest we checked were losing, and this one held on.
First, the reply: something is up for grabs for the other side immediately.
Here's the kicker: the best reply gives check, so the king's safety is the first problem to solve.

You cracked the defense! The position falls without this move, and the human-move model and the alternatives we compared rate it a really tough find. Impressive.
The human-move model had this one penciled in, and the engine agrees it's number one. Obvious and right, the best combo.
Expected by the human-move model, and rated strong by the engine, with one move edging just ahead.

Problem patched: the piece that was unprotected earlier is guarded again.
No single blunder, just small concessions stacking up, and this is another. Let's review the whole stretch.
Edge kept, game won. Nicely finished, all the way to the end.

Check! The king's problem comes first.
The king finds its way out of check.
The pawn arrives on the last rank, and it's promoted on the spot.
New piece on the last rank, and it arrives with check. Neat!
Promotion, and it's checkmate on the spot.
Promotion, and the same move rescues its own king from check.
Capture! A piece comes off.
Take, and check! Double duty from one move.
Take, and that's the game: checkmate.
Grab a piece, dodge the check: this capture does both.
Grab on the last rank, and the pawn becomes a new piece right there.
The pawn captures, promotes, and checks, three things in one move.
Three in one: grab, promote, checkmate, all with a single pawn move.
Capture-and-promote, and its own king gets out of check too.
Castling, and the rook lands on a square that checks the king.
Castling, and the other king is checkmated. Didn't see that coming!
See the fork in action: several targets attacked, then one captured. Tally it up, and this example ends with extra material.
No capture possible: that piece is pinned, with its king farther along the line behind it.
The attacked piece can't run, because it's pinned and its king still needs the shield.
Capture back? Impossible, since the defenders are all stuck shielding their king. In the line shown, that side wins material.
The pinned piece can't leave its post in front of the king. A few moves on, it's captured.
Front piece out of the way, back piece captured on the very same line. Skewer complete.
The king is in check, so it steps aside, and the same attacker grabs what was hiding behind it.
Part one: bye-bye, lone defender. Part two, later in the line: the piece it protected goes too.
The defender gets dragged away from its post, so the piece it was guarding falls.
A blocker moves aside, which opens a line for a different piece to capture.
The blocker hops aside, and boom, the piece behind it is giving check.
Double check! Blocking can't help against two attackers, so the king itself has to move.
Double trouble: the moving piece makes one attack, a hidden piece makes another, and the hidden one is the attack that cashes in.
The pawn promotes, and by this example's last move, that side is still up on material.
That piece had no defender, so it's captured, and in this example the capturing side comes out ahead.
Backstory first: the attacking piece got unpinned. It had been in a relative pin, and the opponent's previous move broke it. The target never moved after that, and the line shown captures it.

A pinned piece wants to move? First peek at what it's shielding: the king, or something worth more than itself.
Spotlight on lines: an attack can go through the first target and land on a bigger prize behind it.
Circle every defender before you trade it off, and ask what it's guarding right now.
When a blocking piece moves, trace every line that just got uncovered.
Circle any move that loads two threats at once. Checks and freshly opened lines are on that list as well.
Quick check before a back-rank defender moves: does the king still have a way out?
Pawn race? Count the moves each pawn needs to promote, and look hard at every forcing push.
Quick check before a defender moves: make a list of its jobs, because those are exactly what it leaves behind.
Do the math on the whole trade: what you take first, plus what the recapture takes back.
Underline this habit: a forcing trade can tug a defender off one job so another job goes undone.
